voiceover: There was a name the people of Israel would not say aloud. Written with four Hebrew consonants, Y H W H, it was the personal name of the God who had spoken to Moses from the fire. When a reader reached it, he said Adonai, Lord, instead. I am the LORD; that is my name, he says through Isaiah. My glory I give to no other. And yet the earliest Christians, Jewish monotheists who guarded that name as jealously as anyone, took the texts that spoke of Yahweh, and applied them to a crucified Galilean. Joel promised that everyone who calls on the name of the LORD shall be saved. There, the Lord upon whose name one calls is Yahweh himself. Paul takes a text about calling on the covenant name of God and, without a word of apology, makes it a text about calling on Jesus. Isaiah 45 is one of the most fiercely monotheistic chapters in all of Scripture. There the LORD swears, to me every knee shall bow. The hymn in Philippians bends that exclusive oath to Jesus. Peter does the same with the reverence Isaiah reserves for God. It is the LORD of hosts whom Israel must honor as holy, now redirected to Christ. And Hebrews takes Psalm 102, a hymn addressed to the eternal Creator, and puts it on the Father's lips as words spoken to the Son: you, Lord, laid the foundation of the earth. A monotheist does not do this by accident, and he does not do it with a creature. To apply the LORD's exclusive oath to Jesus is not to add a second, lesser lord to the picture. That is not the reverence owed a great teacher, or even a supreme angel. Whether any single verse quotes the Name specifically can be debated case by case; the pattern across them is deliberate and hard to explain otherwise. The full case, objections included, is at apologiadaily.com.
